title: She Retired to Care for Family. New Food-Aid Rules Got in the Way
summary:
Lisa Reese worked for nearly 40 years. She worked at a liquor store, cleaned apartments, and worked in hotels. She never got help. Then, at 62, she retired to take care of her family.

Reese lives in Capitol Heights, Maryland, in her family's home. Three generations live there. Her daughter and 2-year-old granddaughter live there too. Daycare cost a lot, so Reese retired to look after everybody.

Reese spent the past 25 years at Marriott. After she left her job, living mostly on Social Security was hard. Prices kept rising, and one gas bill reached $500. This summer, she was approved for food aid from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, known as SNAP. To get $63 a month, she must work, train, or volunteer for 80 hours a month.

The rule is part of big changes to SNAP and Medicaid in a law called the One Big Beautiful Bill. President Trump signed it last year. The law now covers people aged 55 to 64. The Department of Agriculture, which runs SNAP, said the work rule is not punishment.

Reese meets the rule by volunteering at Mission of Love Charities, a nonprofit near her home. Her four-hour morning shift lets her watch her granddaughter in the afternoons. She says the work makes her feel good.
why_it_matters: Rules about food aid can change what food your grandparents or neighbors can buy, and how much time they must spend working or volunteering to get it.
